newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US urges Zaire rulers to probe massacre reports.
newsitem.headline: US urges Zaire rulers to probe massacre reports.

text.p: Top U.S. officials on Thursday urged rebels who took power in former Zaire, renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo, to help probe alleged massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees and to put an end to killings.

John Shattuck, Assistant Secretary of State, and Richard Bogosian, President Bill Clinton's envoy for Africa's Great Lakes region, also told a news conference that Washington was stepping up the pressure on the new rulers to help a U.N. probe.
"Let me express it very clearly here the immediate concern the U.S. government has about reports of the discovery of mass graves in the area in eastern part of Zaire," Shattuck said.
"These reports really call for urgent action and we are at this moment engaged in calling for urgent access to the area by an appropriate U.N. investigative team," he said.

"We are calling upon governments in the region as well as Kinshasa to assist to make sure that that access is given urgently and all reports of killings of refugees are fully investigated and that all killings are stopped."
Widespread reports of massacres in eastern Zaire have brought unsuccessful appeals for an international probe.
Aid officials also voice concern about more recent reports of fresh killings of refugees in camps south of the eastern town of Kisangani where relief workers had been refused access.

But Laurent Kabila's Tutsi-dominated rebels, who ousted veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko and took power in Kinshasa this month, have blocked a U.N. mission with a mandate from the top U.N. rights body to investigate the killings.
Shattuck said Kabila has not kept a promise to the U.S. ambassador to the U.N., Bill Richardson, to authorise the U.N. probe.
He said Washington and other capitals were increasing pressure on the former rebels to do something on human rights.
"We will not stop until that is going to occur," he said.
Washington has been supportive of Kabila and is a political and military ally of neighbouring Rwanda that backed his rebels.

But victory for Kabila has brought little prospect of relief for hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees in a region where centuries-old ethnic hatred between the majority Hutu and minority Tutsi tribes has repeatedly exploded into violence.

The refugees were the rump of two million Rwandans who fled to Zaire in fear of reprisal for the Hutu-led genocide of minority Tutsis in 1994 after which a Tutsi-dominated government swept to power in their tiny central African country.
Bogosian, asked about his assessment of the situation in the east of the country, told Reuters: "It's a big mess."
He said he saw the reports of killings as "not being able to be ignored. The real credible thing is an investigation".
"In eastern Zaire, there is a situation that involves some serious human rights abuses, there's a continuing problem of refugees and that requires attention," he said.
"Obviously, if you have the kind of serious human rights violations that this information suggests, that's going to have some effect on our relationship."

The three-member commission of inquiry was set up in April on the demand of U.N.'s special investigator for Zaire, Roberto Garreton, who said witness reports spoke of as many as 50,000 Hutu refugees and civilians killed by the former rebels.
It must report its findings, which include eyewitness reports of big massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees, to the U.N. General Assembly in New York by June.
"The report will come out, there'll be a big stink about it," said a senior diplomat. "The problem will not go away,"
